title: Three-pile shuffle group
W: Using the six ways to stack three piles in a perfect shuffle, which rearrangements of the deck can you reach? (Already answered.)
M: Determine $G_{3,3n}=\langle \rho_\tau\sigma:\tau\in S_3\rangle\le S_{3n}$. Known answer: $G_{3,3^m}=S_3\wr C_m$; for $n$ not a power of $3$, $G_{3,3n}=S_{3n}$ if $n\not\equiv0\pmod 4$ and $A_{3n}$ if $n\equiv0\pmod4$.
why: Generalises the Diaconis-Graham-Kantor determination of the two-pile perfect-shuffle group; it is the k=3 case of the Medvedoff-Morrison shuffle group conjecture.
issues: Fully solved. Xia-Zhang-Zhang-Zhu (arXiv 2304.01037, Forum Math. Sigma 2024) prove the Medvedoff-Morrison conjecture for all k and give the exact group for k=3 (Thm 1.5): S_3 wr C_m when 3n=3^m, else S_{3n} or A_{3n} by n mod 4. The power-of-k case is due to Medvedoff-Morrison (1987) and Amarra-Morgan-Praeger (arXiv 1908.05128).

title: Monotile assembly threshold
W: (Corrected, already posed.) For tiling simply connected regions with a fixed set of rectangles, two rectangles give a polynomial-time problem while a large set is NP-complete. Do three rectangles suffice for NP-completeness?
M: (Pak-Yang Conjecture 7.5.) Prove there is a set $T$ of three rectangles such that deciding whether a finite simply connected region of $\mathbb Z^2$ can be tiled by translates of tiles from $T$ is NP-complete. (Remila: every two-rectangle set gives a polynomial-time problem.)
why: Locates the exact point where local tiling constraints become computationally universal. It ties tiling theory to the size of the smallest gadgets that can encode SAT.
issues: As stated, the problem is answered or ill-posed. With holes allowed, a single tile (the right tromino) is already NP-complete (Moore-Robson 2001), so t=1, and the 'fewer polygons give P' part is then vacuous. Also, 'NP-complete vs polynomial' is only a dichotomy if P!=NP is assumed. The natural fix (simply connected regions, rectangles) is Pak-Yang's stated Conjecture 7.5 (3 rectangles), so it is not novel. Best known bounds are 111 rectangles / 23 Wang tiles (arXiv 2405.01017) against the lower bound of 3 (Remila).

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
W: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
M: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.
why: Corvaja and Zannier used the Subspace Theorem to show that the greatest prime factor of the product xy over Markov pairs tends to infinity. The single-number version is the natural strengthening. It sits next to the uniqueness conjecture, where Markov numbers that are prime powers are already handled, and to recent strong-approximation work on the Markoff surface.
issues: I found no proof. Single branches are easy: for example, the branch of odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers follows from primitive-divisor theorems. The difficulty is uniformity over the whole tree. Counting does not decide it: there are about (log X)^2 Markov numbers up to X but (log X)^{|S|} S-units, so counting rules out nothing once |S|>=2. A computer check of the 576 Markov numbers up to 1e24 found nothing surprising (smallest largest prime factors above 1000: 53, 61, 109, ...). I did not confirm whether Corvaja-Zannier state the single-number case as open, so novelty is uncertain. The M was made explicit (definition of the set, convention P(1)=1).

title: Ringel for forests
W: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
M: Prove that for every $m\ge1$ and every forest $F$ with $m$ edges, $E(K_{2m+1})$ can be partitioned into $2m+1$ subgraphs each isomorphic to $F$. Stronger form: every such $F$ admits an injective map $f:V(F)\to\mathbb Z_{2m+1}$ whose edge lengths $\min(|f(u)-f(v)|,\,2m+1-|f(u)-f(v)|)$ are exactly $1,\dots,m$ (a $\rho$-labelling).
why: Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov and Keevash-Staden proved Ringel's conjecture for large trees. Their rainbow-copy and cyclic-shift framework does not need connectivity, but the embedding steps do. So the question is whether connectivity is essential to Ringel-type decompositions. A positive answer would be a natural forest analogue of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa theorem.
issues: No counterexample found. A backtracking search found rho-labellings (and hence cyclic decompositions of K_{2m+1}) for all forests without isolated vertices with m<=9 edges (2, 4, 8, 16, 34, 71, 154, 341 forests). I found no paper stating or proving the forest version: MPS, Keevash-Staden and the Glock-Kuhn-Osthus survey treat only trees. A large-m proof may be an adaptation of the existing machinery, which caps the importance. The M was made precise and the rho-labelling strengthening added.

title: Two-frequency localization
W: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
M: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).
why: Multi-frequency localization at large coupling is known only for a full-measure set of frequency vectors, because the proofs (Bourgain-Goldstein, Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag) delete frequencies by semi-algebraic elimination. Proving it for one explicit Diophantine vector such as (√2,√3), which is Diophantine by Schmidt's subspace theorem, would require an arithmetic way to control double resonances, as Jitomirskaya's method does for one frequency.
issues: This is a special case of a recognised open problem (fixed-frequency localization for multi-frequency analytic potentials), not a new question. arXiv 2603.07180 says it is unknown whether some Diophantine frequency can be fixed, and solves only the dual perturbative regime on Z^d. Eliasson (Acta Math 1997) gives pure point spectrum at fixed Diophantine frequency for large Gevrey/analytic couplings, but without exponential decay of eigenfunctions, so the exponential decay is the open content. The original fixed coupling 10 was arbitrary: every known method gives an inexplicit lambda_0, so I replaced it with 'all lambda >= lambda_0'.

title: Rupert superballs
W: A cube can pass through a hole drilled in a copy of itself; a round ball cannot. Show that every superball between them, |x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p ≤ 1 with p > 2, can.
M: Let $B_p=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p+|x_3|^p\le1\}$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Prove that for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are orthogonal projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $\mathbb R^3$ onto planes and a rigid motion $\rho$ with $\rho(\pi_1(B_p))\subset\operatorname{int}\pi_2(B_p)$. By central symmetry this is equivalent to: there are orthonormal pairs $(a_1,a_2),(b_1,b_2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with $\|\cos t\,b_1+\sin t\,b_2\|_q>\|\cos t\,a_1+\sin t\,a_2\|_q$ for all $t$.
why: The Rupert property has been settled for many polyhedra, and a convex polyhedron without it was found in 2025. Smooth, strictly convex bodies are much less studied. The superball family interpolates between the Rupert cube and the non-Rupert ball, so it asks whether any loss of roundness at all creates a passage.
issues: Numerically this looks true and fairly routine. Central symmetry reduces it to comparing q-norms on two planes, with zero translation. Optimisation found positive margins of about 0.0018, 0.007, 0.027, 0.063 and 0.076 at p = 2.05, 2.2, 3, 10 and 60, with the margin growing roughly like 0.035(p-2) near p=2. A proof likely combines first-order perturbation at p=2 (an explicit configuration with positive linearised margin), continuity to the Rupert cube as p→∞, and interval arithmetic in between. That makes it computer-assisted routine work rather than a deep problem. The literature search found no prior treatment of superballs.
